title: Can the courts end Trump's illegal tariffs?
gist: Alan Wolff argues the administration has repeatedly swapped legal bases (IEEPA, Section 122, Section 301 'forced labor') faster than courts can review them, so tariffs likely persist through this administration unless the Supreme Court rules Congress alone holds broad tariff power.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs of 10 percent or higher on February 20, but the 10 percent blanket tariff continued under Section 122 balance-of-payments authority, making the victory hollow beyond refunds.
insights.so_what: Court wins have not lowered the effective tariff wall; IEEPA refunds are the only cash relief.
insights.locator: There was rejoicing in the anti-tariff world
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: The Court of International Trade ruled the Section 122 tariff illegal on May 7 because balance-of-payments tests were not met, but the 150-day authority expired July 24 as the administration moved to a new basis.
insights.so_what: Litigation timelines are shorter than the administration's pivots, rendering rulings largely moot.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: USTR replaced the Section 122 tariff at 12:01 a.m. on July 24, 2026 with Section 301 'forced labor' retaliatory tariffs of at least 10 percent on almost all exporting countries, using a newly created standard none could meet.
insights.so_what: The blanket 10% floor is continuously maintained across legal vehicles.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: The executive branch can impose tariffs instantly and has found means to do so far faster than the courts can review their legitimacy.
insights.so_what: Base case: tariffs persist regardless of individual ruling outcomes.
insights.locator: What we have seen to date
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: The forced labor Section 301 challenge, Burlap and Barrel, Inc. v. United States, is before a three-judge Court of International Trade panel with a ruling expected any day; Wolff, Carla Hills and Warren Maruyama filed an amicus brief arguing Section 301 cannot confer global tariff authority.
insights.so_what: A CIT ruling is an imminent catalyst, though the author expects it to be appealed.
insights.locator: I assume the president will ultimately lose
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: At the September 30 oral argument the judges focused on 1988 Omnibus Trade Act definitions and surprise that forced-labor provisions weren't investigated; the government attorney admitted USTR did not see that language as particularly relevant, which could undermine the case.
insights.so_what: The government's weakness is statutory process, not constitutional, so remand is a plausible outcome.
insights.locator: Oral argument was held on September 30
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: Even if the CIT rules against the government an appeal is likely, and the court is unlikely to enjoin collection because tariff payments are not treated as irreparable harm.
insights.so_what: Tariff collections continue during appeals; do not price an immediate removal.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: Sixteen pending 'excess capacity' Section 301 cases target China, the EU, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, India and others covering 60 to 70 percent of US imports across at least 21 industrial sectors including steel, autos and semiconductors.
insights.so_what: A deeper backup tariff pipeline means winning the forced-labor case would not eliminate tariffs.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: Tariffs will not be eliminated until the Supreme Court states that only Congress holds the power to tax and cannot delegate setting the entire tariff structure to the president; findings that statutes were misapplied are not enough.
insights.so_what: Only a sweeping constitutional ruling ends serial tariff authorities; absent that, tariffs likely last through this administration.
insights.locator: Tariffs will not be eliminated until a court
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: The Roberts court has reached for sweeping results before, as when it ended Chevron deference in Loper Bright v. Raimondo, so the forced labor case is an opportune vehicle, though a sweeping ruling is far from guaranteed.
insights.so_what: Low-probability, high-impact upside scenario for tariff relief.
insights.locator: The court under Chief Justice John Roberts
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff

insights.claim: The Supreme Court chose a technical reading that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs rather than a constitutional ruling, which opened the door for the administration to try again.
insights.so_what: Narrow rulings invite substitution of other statutes.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court could have struck down
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
